source: The Mount’s website (edithwharton.org) and media library

artworks.title: The Stable (1902)
artworks.description: Modeled like the house on Belton House and designed by Hoppin & Koen for the Whartons’ horses and carriages, then their motorcars. “Mr. Wharton’s pride is the stable, which is indeed one of the finest in Lenox” (1904). Today it is The Mount’s main space for talks, readings, music and films, with accessible restrooms.

artworks.title: The Mansion (1902)
artworks.description: Wharton designed the house herself with Ogden Codman Jr. and Francis L. V. Hoppin, built July 1901 – autumn 1902. The outside, by Hoppin, follows Belton House, a 17th-century English country house; the inside follows the rules of Wharton and Codman’s The Decoration of Houses. Four stories on the entrance side, three on the garden side. One of only five percent of National Historic Landmarks dedicated to women.

artworks.title: The Mount on a tinted postcard (c. 1902–03)
artworks.description: The earliest known picture of the finished house, before the gardens were planted.

artworks.title: West elevation by Hoppin & Koen
artworks.description: The architects’ drawing of the entrance front.

artworks.title: The Italian Garden
artworks.description: The sunken walled garden in serene greens and whites, with porticos and alcoves in its stone walls: a cool, shady room against the summer sun. Its centerpiece is a rustic rock-pile fountain. The ramp to it is on the path to the right of the Mansion.

artworks.title: The French Flower Garden
artworks.description: A rectangular pool among beds of annuals, perennials and shrubs: phlox, stocks, lilies, hydrangea, dianthus, delphinium and dahlias, all flowers Wharton loved.

artworks.title: The dolphin fountain
artworks.description: The fountain in the Flower Garden’s pool.

artworks.title: The Lime Walk
artworks.description: A gravel promenade of pleached linden (lime) trees joining the Italian Garden to the French Flower Garden.

artworks.title: The Rock Garden and Grass Steps
artworks.description: A rock garden with Grass Steps molded into the sloping hill, a landscape feature rarely seen in America. Wharton saw her gardens as outdoor rooms in harmony with the house: “Decidedly, I’m a better landscape gardener than novelist.”
artworks.galleryName: The Rock Garden and the Grass Steps

artworks.title: The woods and trails
artworks.description: Meadows, woods and wetlands around the gardens, free to walk from dawn to dusk all year (dogs on leash). Some trails are steep, rough or muddy.
artworks.imageCredit: Stephanie Zollshan for the Berkshire Eagle / The Mount

artworks.title: NightWood (Nov 21, 2026 – Jan 2, 2027)
artworks.description: The Mount’s sound-and-light walk through the woods returns with a longer path: November 21, 25, 27–28; December 4, 5, 11–12, 17–23, 26–31; January 2. Separate ticket, after dark; dress for the weather, no strollers or dogs; uneven terrain with stairs (golf-cart rides at 4:30 pm on some days: 413-551-5111 ext. 5). A NightWood ticket gives 50% off a house tour.

artworks.title: The Entrance Hall
artworks.description: You enter at ground level from the walled Forecourt into a cool, grotto-like hall, meant as an extension of the landscape into the house; the main rooms are a floor above, which gave Wharton privacy from arriving guests. The hall is 34½ by 12½ feet; the staircase hall leads up to the main floor.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The Kitchen
artworks.description: The ground floor of the service wing held the kitchen, a scullery for washing pots and pans, the servants’ dining room and the laundry. The recreated working rooms tell the stories of Wharton’s servants: many served her for decades, others were new immigrants.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The Mount Gift & Bookstore
artworks.description: In the old laundry: books, Wharton titles, jewelry, stationery, teas and toys. Open to everyone, no house ticket needed (May 9–October daily 10–5; November–December weekends 10–3). Phone 413-551-5118.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The Gallery
artworks.description: The 38-foot vaulted hall on the main floor, inspired by the galleries Wharton admired in Italy. It gives each room its own door and lets air flow through the house: Wharton and Ogden Codman’s rule from The Decoration of Houses (1897) that every room should be reached without passing through another.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Teddy Wharton’s Den
artworks.description: Edward (Teddy) Wharton’s office, 15 by 18 feet, with French doors. A “hidden” door in the bookcase leads straight into his wife’s Library.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Edith Wharton’s Library
artworks.description: The oak-paneled library holds Wharton’s own books, about 2,700 volumes the house bought back in 2005: books from every period of her life in English, French, German and Italian, many of her own works with penciled corrections, and books inscribed by friends. She marked them gently in pencil: ticks, underlining, sometimes words. Private library tours by reservation ($150 for two).
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Fighting France: From Dunkerque to Belfort
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: Wharton’s account of her journeys into the war zones of France with Walter Berry, inscribed by her to her chauffeur Charles Cook, who drove them. Cook, from Lenox, joined the household in 1903 and drove the Whartons for nearly twenty years; The Mount bought this copy in 2020.
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: Leaves of Grass
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: Heavily marked and fragile from use, given to Wharton in 1898 by Walter Berry, who wrote in it a line of “Song of Myself”: “Who can stray from me? I follow you whoever you are from the present hour.” When Berry died in 1927 Wharton wrote, “all my life goes with him.”
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: The Age of Innocence
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: Wharton’s own copy of her Pulitzer Prize novel, with her bookplate from Sainte-Claire-du-Château. She made about 30 corrections between the first and sixth printings. Given back to The Mount by Dennis and Andrea Kahn in 2020, the novel’s centenary.
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: Misrepresentative Women
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: Light verse, a gift from Henry James, inscribed “To a much misrepresented woman from the largest of her admirers.” A favorite of visitors to the library.
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: Poems
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: The only book by Meynell in Wharton’s library, with John Singer Sargent’s portrait of the poet. It contains “Renouncement,” a favorite of Wharton’s, which she chose for her anthology Eternal Passion in English Poetry.
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: Poems
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: Given to Wharton at 19. She marked two lines of “Resignation” and quoted them to Morton Fullerton in 1908: “They, believe me, who await no gifts from chance, have conquered fate.”
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: Lays of the Scottish Cavaliers
artworks.medium: Book from Edith Wharton’s own library
artworks.description: A present for Edith’s 14th birthday from her sister-in-law Minnie Cadwalader Jones, a friend for life.
artworks.placeNote: Kept in Wharton’s Library. The books are seen from the doorway on the house tour; to look inside them, book a private library tour.

artworks.title: The Drawing Room
artworks.description: The largest room in the house, 36 by 20 feet, opening onto the Terrace and the gardens. Wharton and Codman planned its proportion and symmetry down to the doors: “Before beginning to decorate a room it is essential to consider for what purpose the room is to be used.”
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The Dining Room
artworks.description: A small, intimate room, 20½ by 25½ feet, opening onto the Terrace. The only photograph from the Whartons’ time shows a round table with white-painted French armchairs; the room has been re-created.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The Butler’s Pantry
artworks.description: On the main floor, the servants worked in the butler’s pantry, the brush room (for cleaning shoes and outdoor wear) and the offices of household management.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.
artworks.galleryName: Butler’s pantry and the passage to the service wing

artworks.title: The Terrace and Terrace Café
artworks.description: The Italian-inspired terrace, 125 feet long along the garden front, which Wharton asked for; a Palladian staircase leads down to the gardens. In season the Terrace Café (KJ Nosh) serves sandwiches, salads, wine and beer, first come, first served; no ticket needed. Closed for the season now.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.
artworks.galleryName: The Terrace and the Terrace Café

artworks.title: Edith Wharton’s Boudoir
artworks.description: Her private sitting room, next to her bedroom and bath at the north end of the bedroom floor.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Edith Wharton’s Bedroom
artworks.description: Wharton’s bedroom at the north end of the house. She preferred to write in bed in the mornings rather than in her library; she wrote The House of Mirth (1905) at The Mount.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: The West Guest Suite
artworks.description: A two-room guest suite with its bath on the west side, over the Forecourt.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Teddy Wharton’s Bedroom
artworks.description: Teddy Wharton’s bedroom, bath and dressing room on the east side, smaller than his wife’s.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.
artworks.galleryName: Teddy Wharton’s bedroom, bath and dressing room

artworks.title: The Henry James Suite
artworks.description: The largest guest bedroom, on the east side, known by the name of its most famous guest. Henry James stayed at The Mount in 1904 and 1905; Wharton called him “perhaps the most intimate friend I ever had.”
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.

artworks.title: Exhibits on the third floor
artworks.description: Informational exhibits about Wharton, her house and her household. They are not on the audio guide; staff can help with reading them (413-551-5116). Which rooms they fill isn’t published: ask on the tour.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.
artworks.galleryName: Rooms with The Mount’s informational exhibits

artworks.title: The Sewing Room
artworks.description: On the bedroom floor of the service wing: the sewing room, a closet for Wharton’s dresses, a linen closet and her personal maid’s room. The wheelchair lift to the rest of the floor is here, first room on the right from the elevator.
artworks.placeNote: Room shapes on the map are approximate: The Mount publishes no floor plan.
artworks.galleryName: Sewing Room and Wharton’s dress closet
